Subject: Pilot extension request — exchangeable hours vs flat bid

Hi Rishi,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the team found the latency and cost profiles promising. We’re approaching the end of our 30-day pilot and would like to extend the evaluation by ~3 weeks to complete inference accuracy tests across more traffic.

Before we proceed I wanted to float two commercial approaches and get your take:

1) Exchangeable hours: We top up the pilot with 4,500 GPU hours (exchangeable across models/regions during the pilot).
2) Flat bid: A fixed three-week flat fee that covers a capped throughput (e.g., up to X concurrent sessions), simpler for procurement.

Given the pilot stage, could Redwood provide a modest extension discount (we were hoping for something in the 15–25% range) and confirm whether unused hours (option 1) could convert to credits against a first quarter committed purchase? Also, our procurement folks will need a draft PO/statement of work to move quickly.

Two operational asks as well: can you hold short-term SLA for p95 response under 800ms during the extension, and include an attachment with the usage report you’ve seen so far?

Appreciate a rough sketch of numbers so we can move to internal approval.

Best,
Ben
Head of ML Ops
Quantly

Hi Ben — thanks for the clear framing, and glad the demo was useful. Short answers up front: we can support both commercial approaches, and we can supply a draft PO addendum for procurement. A couple of clarifying points below so we can price it accurately.

Commercial options (ballpark):
- Exchangeable hours: $0.45 / GPU-hour list, tiered to $0.36 / GPU-hour at 4,500 hours (20% discount). Unused hours convert to credits valid for 90 days, applied to the first committed order.
- Flat bid (3 weeks): $38,000 flat (covers up to 250 concurrent sessions during the pilot); includes one prioritized incident response window per week.

We prefer the exchangeable-hours route when the work pattern is spiky; flat bid is cleaner for procurement. For either option we can provide a one-time extension discount of 15% off the figure above (applies to startups during pilot extensions). If Quantly agrees to a Q1 committed minimum (discussed after the pilot), we can increase that to 20%.

On the SLA: our hosted tier does not offer hard latency SLAs on shared capacity. For guaranteed p95/p99 targets we recommend Redwood Dedicated or a short-term capacity reservation for the pilot extension (technical note: Dedicated changes the pricing shape). If you want us to propose a short-term Dedicated window for the three weeks, I’ll loop in David to confirm feasibility and costs.

I’ll draft a PO addendum and include the usage report we have on file. Laura — can you prep a PO/contract sketch and include language for unused-hour credits? Hannah — can you confirm the discount runway (15% vs 20% contingent)?

Rishi

Quick technical note on the SLA ask:

- Hosted (shared) tier: we cannot offer a contractual p95 latency SLA for shared capacity — noisy neighbors and autoscaling behavior make hard SLAs risky. We can operationally prioritize their account for the extension window (engineer-on-call, dedicated queue) but it’s not a formal SLA.

- Dedicated window (recommended for SLA): we can reserve 1x A100 equivalent pod and set a short-term capacity reservation for the three-week pilot extension. Estimated uplift: +32% on the exchangeable-hours rate (due to reserved capacity overhead). That means the effective unit cost would move from $0.36/hr to roughly $0.48/hr for reserved pods.

- Tradeoffs: Dedicated guarantees latency profile and isolation (good for p95 targets), but procurement will see higher line-items. If Quantly needs evidence for procurement, we can produce a short runbook and an ops agreement (two-page) describing the reserved window.

Happy to run the sizing if Ben can share the peak concurrent sessions and an expected token/sec distribution.

-David
Senior Infrastructure Engineer
Redwood Inference
